title: Support productive struggle in learning mathematics
subtitle: Let students wrestle with ideas that are within reach but not yet easy — and resist the urge to rescue them out of the very thinking that builds understanding.

sections.sources: Source: NCTM, Principles to Actions (2014) · Hiebert & Grouws · Adding It Up (2001).

blocks.text: Effective teaching consistently provides students, individually and collectively, with opportunities and supports to engage in productive struggle as they grapple with mathematical ideas and relationships.

Struggle is **productive** when the task is within reach and the effort is building understanding — it is where learning actually happens. The instinct to remove all difficulty is well-meant but counterproductive: over-scaffolding hands students the answer and takes the learning with it. The teacher’s craft is to keep students in the struggle while giving *just enough* support to keep it productive rather than destructive.
What it looks like in grades 6–8

items: A classroom norm that being stuck is normal and expected — “stuck is where we learn.”
The teacher responding to “I’m stuck” with a question, not the next step.
Wait time and think time held even when it’s uncomfortable.
Support that keeps the demand: “what have you tried?” rather than “here, do this.”

yes.title: We want to see & hear
items: “This is supposed to feel hard — keep going”
The teacher asking a question instead of rescuing
Mistakes treated as information, not failure

no.title: We should *not* see
items: Hints that dissolve the problem at the first sigh
The teacher stepping in within seconds of a pause
Struggle framed as “you don’t get it”
Tasks pre-chewed until no thinking is left

blocks.text: Where it lives in our toolbelt

Productive struggle is the point of [Rich Tasks](/math/approach/rich-tasks) and [Thin-Slicing](/math/approach/thin-slicing), protected by [vertical surfaces & random groups](/math/approach/vnps) (more starts, less hiding). The [When to Tell](/math/approach/when-to-tell) guide is precisely the judgment call this practice demands — support without dissolving the struggle.
When a student says “I’m stuck,” count to three and answer with a question: “what have you tried?” or “what do you know so far?” Keep the pencil in their hand.
